results.summary: This design selects one of six ring oscillators or the system clock and divides the chosen frequency by 10 and 100. It outputs a 5-bit Gray-coded decimal value representing the divided count. The design is intended as a test structure for characterizing ring oscillators on the ASIC. It requires no external hardware beyond the clock and provides a way to observe oscillator behavior through the divided outputs.

This project implements a TOTP authenticator that generates 6 to 8 digit codes for two-factor authentication, compatible with common apps like Google Authenticator. It accepts a shared secret and timestamp via a serial input and displays the generated code on a 7-segment display. Debug outputs are available on the bidirectional pins for inspecting internal SHA1 and HMAC operations. The design is documented only by its pin names and a TODO placeholder, so detailed operation and testing procedures are not provided.

QTCore-A1 is an accumulator-based 8-bit microprocessor with a Von Neumann architecture, designed for Tiny Tapeout 3.5. It includes a control unit, program counter, instruction register, accumulator, and 19 bytes of memory, all accessible via a scan chain. The processor is programmed and controlled through an external microcontroller's SPI interface, using the SPI clock to drive both the scan chain and the processor. Notably, all functional Verilog was generated by GPT-4 through conversation, with human-written testbenches used for validation.

This is a simple loopback test module that mirrors input 0 to outputs 0 through 6, and outputs the logical AND of inputs 4 through 7 on output 7. It is used to verify signal integrity and timing by toggling input 0 and measuring the delay until the corresponding outputs change. The design requires no external hardware beyond the input signals. It serves as a basic infrastructure test for the Tiny Tapeout 3.5 shuttle.

SPINet is a network-on-chip designed to connect microcontroller clusters via SPI. It provides SPI interfaces for up to four nodes, with handshake signals for data flow control. The design is documented with a reference to an external video for background, but the on-chip documentation is minimal. Testing instructions are not provided, so users must infer operation from pin names and the external reference.

The M0 is a 16-bit bit-serial microprocessor based on the SUBLEQ architecture, requiring external SPI RAM and ROM for operation. It includes a transmit UART for serial output and interoperates with Oleg Mazonka's HSQ C-compiler for SUBLEQ. The design can be tested without RAM/ROM by observing SPI clock patterns and UART output, or with external memory for full program execution. Notable for fitting a capable processor into a very small area, though it operates slowly due to its bit-serial nature.

This is a power test module that replicates the standard Tiny Tapeout test design but includes a PMOS transistor to control power to the module. The PMOS requires an external active-low enable signal. The design passes input signals directly to outputs, allowing verification that outputs toggle when power is enabled. It is used to evaluate the power switching FET on the TT03p5 shuttle.

This project is a guitar tuner that measures the frequency of input pulses and displays the result on a 7-segment display. It uses clock dividers and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for the display, and outputs a slower square wave on output 7. The design is documented with a TODO placeholder, so detailed operation and testing are not fully described. It requires an external signal representing the frequency to be measured.

This design is a ring oscillator with a 64-bit counter that counts oscillations, gated by a PFET for power switching tests. The counter value can be shifted out via inputs, and the counter can be reset or stopped. It is used to evaluate the power switching FET on the TT03p5 shuttle. The design requires no external hardware beyond control signals.

This design implements a 4-trit balanced ternary program counter with up, down, and hold counting modes, as well as jump/load capability. It also includes a 3-trit asynchronous balanced ternary radix converter that converts to signed binary and back. The design is written in MRCS and tests the capabilities of the MRCS Verilog generator and Tiny Tapeout's bidirectional pins. It is verified on an FPGA with a provided testbench, and the ASIC version is functionally similar.
